The harness requires equivalent GPU types and a small pre‑warm period to produce stable P99s.

Key constraints:
- Hardware affects slope: consumer‑grade A100 vs. A800/RTX show different plateau behavior once batching/kv cache saturates.
- Warm‑up: KV cache & prefix cache must be warmed for steady-state; raw cold-start numbers are included but we highlight steady-state.
- Mixed workload: our standard mixed test uses 60% short-chat (<=64 tokens) + 30% medium (65–512 tokens) + 10% long (512–2048 tokens).

Lisa — quick operational notes and the exact parameters we used for the sample curves (so you can reproduce):

Sample harness summary (bullets so it can go into the RFP):
- Test runner: redwood-loadgen v1.4 (open harness README attached).
- Models: public-redwood-v1-large (float16), 4/8‑GPU config equivalent (we indicate per‑GPU PERF metrics in CSV).
- Workload mix: 60% short (<=64 tokens), 30% medium (65–512), 10% long (512–1024).
- Concurrency sweep: linear steps from 1 -> 8 -> 16 -> 32 -> 64 -> 128 -> 256 (per‑instance concurrent in-flight requests).
- Batch formation: continuous batching with 20ms max hold, dynamic batch cap at 64 tokens.
- Warm‑up: 300s warm window (requests sent at 10% of target QPS) followed by 600s steady-state window for each concurrency point.
- Metrics captured: end‑to‑end latency distribution (P50/P90/P95/P99/P99.9), server CPU/GPU utilization, token/sec, mean GPU mem utilization, and KV cache hit ratio.

Why this helps reproduce numbers: the warm‑up window ensures KV cache and prefix cache reach steady state; the continuous batch hold limits variance from micro batching; concurrency points capture plateaus and knee points for autoscaling.

CSV artifact contents: per concurrency step we provide columns: concurrency, qps, mean_tokens_per_sec, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, p999_ms, gpu_util_pct, kv_cache_hit_pct. We also include hardware labels and config hash for reproducibility.

Notes on differences you might see when re-running: small variance (<5%) in p50/p95 when using production traces instead of our synthetic mixing; P99 is sensitive to burstiness in traces and requires longer observation windows to smooth.

If you want, we can include a parity checklist for your team to ensure run parity (e.g., same model weights, identical tokenizer commit, same seq-limits).

-Vanessa
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Adding a couple of engineering details that teams often miss when attempting an apples-to-apples re-run:

1) Measurement boundaries: define whether latency is measured at the client (end-to-end) or at the model forward time. Our CSV includes both E2E and model-forward (server) latencies and we surface the model-forward for kernel tuning.

2) Token accounting: report tokens/sec as decoded tokens (post-tokenizer). For batching studies, prefer tokens/sec per GPU to normalize across hardware.

3) GPU telemetry: capture SM utilization, power draw, and memory bandwidth. We correlate tail latency spikes with GPU PCIe stalls and kernel preemption events — we provide example logs with annotated TTL spikes.

4) Quantization & fallback: if you test an INT8/4-bit quantized variant, report both quality deltas and latency deltas. Our scaling curves include an optional quantized trace so you can compare. Fallbacks (for example, switching from quantized to fp16 on mismatch) will change the right‑hand plateau of the curve.

5) Recommended curve format: provide concurrency on X (log scale optional), plot qps and p99 on Y (secondary axis for p99). Also include a normalized cost axis (tokens/sec per $) if you want to compare economics.

I'll attach a short snippet (in the README) with the exact perf counters and the parsing commands we use. Happy to walk your infra team through the logs during the workshop.

-Priyom
